newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Blazing sheep ship still missing in Indian Ocean.
newsitem.headline: Blazing sheep ship still missing in Indian Ocean.

text.p: A blazing, abandoned ship with almost 70,000 live Australian sheep on board has gone missing somewhere in the Seychelles area of the Indian Ocean, officials said on Friday.
"It's a fairly evocative instance when live animals are involved," Robin Poke, spokesman for the Australian Maritime Safety Authority (AMSA), told Reuters on Friday.

The vessel still had not been found five hours after a rescue tug from the Gulf of Aden and a converted car carrier from Karachi reached the area where the ship had been abandoned, an Australian Meat and Livestock Corp (AMLC) official said.

The 14,990 tonne, Panama-flagged ship Uniceb left Fremantle in the state of Western Australia on August 23 on a routine 16-day run with 67,000 live sheep to Australia's biggest live sheep market, Jordan.
But 400 km (245 miles) east of the Seychelles off the north African coast, an engine room fire quickly spread to the crew's quarters, killing one of the ship's 55-member crew.

The remaining crew of 22 Filipinos, 17 Chileans and 15 Indians abandoned the ship and were picked up by a passing cargo vessel. The Uniceb is owned by Sistrin Services, based in the Swiss town of Lugano.
The missing Uniceb threatens to be Australia's worst live sheep disaster, although the number of sheep on board is far fewer than the maximimum normal shipment of 120,000.
In 1980, 40,600 sheep were lost in a fire on a ship travelling from the Australian island state of Tasmania to Iran.

The Uniceb incident has caused a furore in Australia, with animal welfare groups and unionists calling for an end to the live trade. But livestock officials and politicians are adamant that the trade is worth too much to close it down.

Australian live sheep and cattle exports have grown over the past three decades to about A$500 million (US$395 million) a year. Australia exported 5.54 million live sheep last year, most to the Middle East, worth A$208 million,
"It's an extremely unfortunate accident. We've got a good safety record and hopefully long-term, we'll be able to continue to show that," said AMLC spokesman Chris Rowley.
Lloyd Beeby, head of the AMLC's live sheep marketing division, strongly defended Australia's safety and humanitarian record in its live animal trade.
Livestock vessels must conform with stringent requirements laid down by the Australian Maritime Safety Authority and by an industry-government panel, Beeby said.
Ships in recent years have been refused the right to export live animals from Australia because they did not meet AMSA requirements, he said.
Sheep aboard ships are transported in pens, whose size and shape vary according to the configuration of the vessel.

Pens varried from two metres by two metres (six feet by six feet) up to 10 metres by three metres (30 feet by nine feet), with the number of sheep per pen varying according to the size of sheep and the amount of wool they carried.
Pens could contain 20 to 30 sheep or more than 100. The walls of pens do not necessarily run from floor to ceiling.

Water was delivered to the sheep through automatic pump techniques. In some ships feeding is performed automatically, while in others, feed was dropped from the roof through chutes on each deck, then transported by wheelbarrows by the crew.
Beeby said he could not comment on the specific systems used on the Uniceb.
